newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Nigerian ships begin attack on S.Leone coup leaders.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian ships begin attack on S.Leone coup leaders.

text.p: Nigerian naval vessels began an attack on Monday to restore Sierra Leone's ousted civilian president hours after the new military strongman went ahead with naming his ruling council.

The booming of naval guns shook the capital at 6 A.M. (0600 GMT) as Nigerian vessels opened fire. The target was not immediately clear and there was no sign of explosions near the coup leaders' headquarters.
"The attack has started," said a West African military official in the capital.
There was no indication of fighting on the ground. The street outside the hotel where most remaining foreigners in the capital had sheltered was quiet.

The attack followed a Sunday radio broadcast in which Major Johnny Paul Koromah announced his 20-member council, with rebel leader Foday Sankoh as vice chairman and including three more members of Sankoh's Revolutionary United Front (RUF).

Koromah was the highest ranked of the original coup leaders but his policy-making body includes three brigadiers and four colonels, plus a few civilians, including the secretary-general of the government and the attorney-general.

A senior Western diplomat, confident a negotiated restoration of the government was still likely, said on Sunday the announcement of the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council was meant to reassure the army's lower ranks and the RUF rebel movement that opposed negotiations.

"We expect an agreement to be reached and if the RUF opposes it, the regional force will go for them," he said. Nigeria, Ghana and Guinea have sent troops ready for a military strike if the talks fail.
Nigerian troops in Sierra Leone came under fire from rebels on Sunday on the highway into the capital from Hastings airport to the east of town. No one was hurt.
British High Commissioner Peter Penfold and Nigerian High Commissioner Chidi Abubakar had hosted secret preliminary talks culminating in a comprehensive meeting on Sunday.
A senior diplomat said Sankoh's rebels, who have been fighting a bush war since 1991 and have allied with the coupmakers, opposed a settlement and had not been part of the negotiations.

Diplomats said the RUF's resistance to a deal had led to serious rifts between its commanders and the coup leaders. Sierra Leonean sources said two people had been killed in gunfights between RUF rebels and soldiers inside Koromah's military headquarters on a Freetown beachfront.
On Sunday U.S. helicopters evacuated the last Americans and Europeans who had taken refuge in two beachside hotels from the violence which followed the coup.
Britain chartered a DC10 to fly some 230 British evacuees from the Guinean capital Conakry to London's Stansted airport.

Among the first to emerge when the plane landed early on Monday were three-year-old twins Daphne and Desphelia Lewis, who had returned to Britain alone, the British Press Association news agency reported.
The agency quoted British missionary Christine Jones, 49, as saying: "It was getting more and more tense by the time we got out on a French naval ship on Saturday.
"Since the situation became international, people who are not Sierra Leone nationals have become targets and homes are being looted.
"I saw a lot of shooting. I saw bodies and I saw shops just being cleared out. For quite a while I thought I would not get out alive."
